items.stimulus: The museum describes its new exhibit as a "free" experience, meaning visitors may explore its rooms in any order they choose. Yet the museum charges admission to the exhibit. So the museum's description is false.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: treats a word used in one sense in the museum's description as if it were used in a different sense
options.why: The museum meant "free to explore in any order"; the argument reads it as "no charge."

options.text: concludes that a claim is false merely because it has not been proven true
options.why: The argument offers a reason (the admission charge), not a lack of proof.

options.text: assumes that what is true of the exhibit is true of the museum as a whole
options.why: The argument makes no claim about the museum as a whole.

options.text: relies on the testimony of museum staff who may have a motive to mislead
options.why: No testimony is cited.

options.text: fails to consider that admission prices may change in the future
options.why: Future prices don't bear on whether the description was false.

items.tldr: "Free" meant free to wander, not free of charge, so the charge doesn't make the description false.

steps.label: Spot the word
steps.body: The whole argument turns on "free."

steps.label: Compare senses
steps.body: The museum's sense is about movement; the critic's sense is about price.

items.takeaway: When an argument turns on a single word, check whether it keeps the same meaning throughout.

items.stimulus: Columnist: Greenfield's mayor is the most trustworthy official in the region. After all, she has never told the public anything false, and we can be confident of that because a trustworthy official like her would never mislead the public.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is flawed because it

options.text: attacks the character of the mayor's critics rather than their arguments
options.why: No critics are mentioned.

options.text: takes for granted that the mayor's popularity proves her trustworthiness
options.why: Popularity never comes up.

options.text: confuses a necessary condition for trustworthiness with a sufficient one
options.why: The problem is circularity, not a conditional reversal.

options.text: draws a conclusion about all officials from the case of a single official
options.why: The conclusion is about the mayor alone.

options.text: presupposes the truth of its conclusion in offering support for one of its premises
options.why: Her honesty is "shown" by assuming she's trustworthy, which is the conclusion itself.

items.tldr: It proves she's trustworthy by assuming she's trustworthy. That's circular.

steps.label: Trace support
steps.body: Conclusion ← she never lied ← a trustworthy official wouldn't lie.

steps.label: Notice
steps.body: The last link assumes the conclusion, so nothing independent supports it.

items.takeaway: If a premise only makes sense once you accept the conclusion, the argument is circular.

items.stimulus: Either the city raises property taxes or it closes two of its public libraries. Since raising property taxes would hurt the city's homeowners, the city should close the libraries.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: treats a claim about the city's budget as if it were a claim about its residents
options.why: The argument doesn't blur those claims.

options.text: assumes that whatever hurts homeowners also hurts renters
options.why: Renters are never mentioned.

options.text: fails to consider that there may be options other than raising property taxes or closing libraries
options.why: The city might cut other spending, find grants or raise other fees.

options.text: relies on an appeal to popular opinion
options.why: No one's opinion is cited.

options.text: draws a general conclusion from a single example
options.why: No example is used.

items.tldr: It assumes those are the only two choices.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Tax or close libraries; tax hurts homeowners; so close libraries.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: The "either/or" premise ignores every other way to balance the budget.

items.takeaway: "Either X or Y" premises are suspect: ask whether there's a third option.

items.stimulus: Dr. Lim, a renowned cardiologist, says that the new tax on sugary drinks will have no effect on the local economy. So the tax will have no effect on the local economy.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses what will happen with what should happen
options.why: Both claims are about what will happen.

options.text: attacks Dr. Lim's motives instead of evaluating her claim
options.why: The argument accepts her claim; it doesn't attack her.

options.text: relies on the opinion of an expert on a matter outside her area of expertise
options.why: A cardiologist's training doesn't make her an authority on economics.

options.text: assumes that a tax that affects health will also affect the economy
options.why: The argument concludes there will be no economic effect.

options.text: treats a correlation as evidence of causation
options.why: No correlation is cited.

items.tldr: A heart specialist's view on economics isn't expert evidence.

steps.label: Source
steps.body: The only support is Dr. Lim's say-so.

steps.label: Fit
steps.body: Her expertise (cardiology) doesn't cover the claim (economic effects).

items.takeaway: Expert testimony counts only within the expert's field.

items.stimulus: A recent poll found that 70 percent of residents believe the proposed highway will reduce traffic downtown. Since so many residents agree, the highway will reduce downtown traffic.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: assumes that reducing traffic is the highway's only purpose
options.why: The argument doesn't discuss the highway's purposes.

options.text: fails to consider that the highway's costs may outweigh its benefits
options.why: The conclusion is about traffic, not whether the highway is worth it.

options.text: treats the fact that many people believe a claim as sufficient evidence that it is true
options.why: Widespread belief about traffic isn't evidence about traffic.

options.text: relies on a poll of residents who do not live downtown
options.why: The stimulus doesn't say where the respondents live.

options.text: confuses a cause with an effect
options.why: No causal reversal occurs.

items.tldr: Seventy percent believing it doesn't make it true.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The only support is what most residents believe.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: Belief, however common, isn't evidence that the belief is correct.

items.takeaway: Popularity is evidence of opinion, not of fact.

items.stimulus: Councilor Diaz has proposed lowering the speed limit on Elm Street from 35 to 25 miles per hour. But banning cars from Elm Street entirely would devastate the businesses there. Diaz's proposal should therefore be rejected.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: concludes that a proposal will fail merely because it has not been tried
options.why: Novelty isn't the stated reason.

options.text: argues against a position more extreme than the one actually proposed
options.why: Diaz proposed a lower speed limit, not a ban on cars.

options.text: assumes that what benefits businesses also benefits residents
options.why: Residents' interests never come up.

options.text: attacks Diaz's character rather than her proposal
options.why: It attacks a (distorted) proposal, not Diaz herself.

options.text: relies on a sample that is unrepresentative
options.why: No sample is involved.

items.tldr: It refutes a car ban nobody proposed. That's a straw man.

steps.label: Proposal
steps.body: Lower the limit from 35 to 25.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Rebuts a total ban, a much stronger position, then rejects the real proposal.

items.takeaway: Check whether the view being attacked is the view actually held.

items.stimulus: Last month I ate at two restaurants in Port Ellis, and both served undercooked fish. Clearly, the restaurants in Port Ellis do not follow food-safety standards.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: relies on a source with a stake in the outcome
options.why: No interested source is involved.

options.text: draws a broad conclusion about a group on the basis of too few cases
options.why: Two meals can't show what all of the town's restaurants do.

options.text: mistakes a lack of evidence for evidence that something is false
options.why: The argument cites positive evidence, just too little of it.

options.text: confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one
options.why: No conditional reasoning appears.

options.text: presumes that what is true of a group is true of each of its members
options.why: The argument runs from members to the group, not the reverse.

items.tldr: Two restaurants can't speak for every restaurant in town.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Two bad meals at two restaurants.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: A claim about all the town's restaurants, which is far broader than the evidence.

items.takeaway: Watch the gap between how many cases are cited and how broad the conclusion is.

items.stimulus: No study has ever shown that the herbal supplement Calmera improves sleep. Therefore, Calmera does not improve sleep.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses improving sleep with curing insomnia
options.why: Insomnia isn't mentioned.

options.text: takes the lack of evidence for a claim as proof that the claim is false
options.why: No study showing an effect isn't the same as studies showing no effect.

options.text: relies on studies funded by the supplement's manufacturer
options.why: No studies are cited at all.

options.text: generalizes from a small number of studies
options.why: The point is that there are no supporting studies.

options.text: assumes that what helps some people sleep helps everyone sleep
options.why: The argument makes no claim about who is helped.

items.tldr: "Not shown to work" doesn't mean "shown not to work."

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: No evidence that it works.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: It doesn't work, which needs evidence against it, not just missing evidence for it.

items.takeaway: Absence of proof is not proof of absence.

items.stimulus: The proposed factory could release pollutants into the Redwater River. Pollution in the river would harm the fish that local anglers depend on. So if the factory is built, the anglers' catch will decline.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: treats something that could happen as if it will happen
options.why: The factory "could" pollute, but the conclusion says the catch "will" decline.

options.text: confuses a cause of pollution with an effect of pollution
options.why: The causal chain runs in a sensible direction.

options.text: fails to weigh the factory's economic benefits
options.why: The conclusion is about the catch, not overall worth.

options.text: concludes that a factory is harmful merely because it is new
options.why: The argument gives a reason beyond newness.

options.text: relies on the testimony of anglers who oppose the factory
options.why: No anglers are quoted.

items.tldr: "Could pollute" becomes "will reduce the catch." A possibility is treated as certain.

steps.label: Find the hedge
steps.body: "Could release pollutants."

steps.label: Find the jump
steps.body: "Will decline" assumes the pollution actually happens.

items.takeaway: Watch for "may" or "could" in the premises and "will" in the conclusion.

items.stimulus: Shortly after the town of Millbrook painted its fire hydrants bright yellow, the number of house fires in Millbrook declined. Evidently, the yellow paint helped prevent house fires.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: infers that one event caused another merely because the second followed the first
options.why: Fires declining after the painting doesn't show the painting caused the decline.

options.text: assumes that yellow is the only color that would have helped
options.why: The argument never compares colors.

options.text: presumes that hydrants are used to fight every house fire
options.why: That presumption isn't needed for the argument as stated.

options.text: attacks the motives of those who opposed painting the hydrants
options.why: No opponents appear.

options.text: confuses the number of fires with the damage they cause
options.why: Damage isn't discussed.

items.tldr: Before-and-after timing alone doesn't show the paint did anything.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Paint, then fewer fires.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: Sequence isn't cause. Weather, inspections or chance could explain the drop.

items.takeaway: "After this, therefore because of this" is a flaw. Look for a rival explanation.

items.stimulus: To cut its carbon emissions by 20 percent, the Halcyon Corporation must stop operating its oldest factory, since that factory produces 20 percent of the company's emissions.
items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument?

options.text: It relies on emissions figures supplied by the company itself.
options.why: The source of the figures isn't mentioned.

options.text: It concludes that the company will close the factory merely because it should.
options.why: The argument says the company must close it, not that it will.

options.text: It assumes that the oldest factory is also the least profitable.
options.why: Profit never comes up.

options.text: It treats a reduction in emissions as a reduction in every kind of pollution.
options.why: Only emissions are discussed.

options.text: It overlooks the possibility that the company could cut emissions by the same amount in other ways.
options.why: Closing that factory is one way to hit 20 percent, not the only one.

items.tldr: Closing that factory is one way to cut 20 percent, not the only way.

steps.label: Claim
steps.body: "Must" close the factory to reach the goal.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: Efficiency upgrades or cuts elsewhere could reach the same 20 percent.

items.takeaway: "Must" claims about reaching a goal often ignore other routes to it.

items.stimulus: To be admitted to the Bellmont Conservatory, an applicant must pass a rigorous audition. Theo passed the audition, so he will be admitted to the conservatory.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: draws a conclusion about all applicants from one applicant's case
options.why: The conclusion is about Theo only.

options.text: relies on Theo's own report that he passed
options.why: The stimulus states that he passed.

options.text: presumes that the audition is the conservatory's only requirement for graduation
options.why: Graduation isn't the issue; the argument is about admission.

options.text: treats a requirement for admission as if it guaranteed admission
options.why: Passing is necessary, but other requirements could still keep Theo out.

options.text: assumes that every applicant who fails the audition will reapply
options.why: Reapplying isn't discussed.

items.tldr: "Must pass to get in" doesn't mean "passing gets you in."

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Admitted → passed audition. Theo passed, so the argument concludes Theo is admitted.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That reverses the conditional, treating a requirement as a guarantee.

items.takeaway: "Must" introduces a necessary condition. Meeting it isn't enough.

items.stimulus: The Westfield Symphony won this year's statewide orchestra competition. So each of its musicians must be among the best musicians in the state.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: confuses the orchestra's past success with its future success
options.why: No prediction is made.

options.text: treats a competition result as if it were a matter of opinion
options.why: The argument takes the result as fact.

options.text: assumes that a property of a whole group must belong to each of its members
options.why: An orchestra can win as an ensemble even if some individual players aren't top-tier.

options.text: assumes that a property of each member must belong to the whole group
options.why: That's the opposite direction. This argument runs from the group to each member.

options.text: generalizes from a single performance to the orchestra's entire history
options.why: The conclusion is about the musicians, not the orchestra's history.

items.tldr: The best orchestra needn't consist entirely of the best musicians.

steps.label: Direction
steps.body: Whole (the orchestra won) to parts (each musician is the best).

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That's division. Group success can come from teamwork or a few stars.

items.takeaway: What's true of a group isn't automatically true of each member.

items.stimulus: This year, 40 percent of the cars sold at Avalon Motors were electric, up from 25 percent last year. So Avalon Motors sold more electric cars this year than last year.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: assumes that electric cars are more profitable than other cars
options.why: Profit isn't mentioned.

options.text: presumes that the customers who bought electric cars were satisfied
options.why: Satisfaction isn't part of the argument.

options.text: relies on sales figures from only two years
options.why: Comparing two years is fine. The issue is shares versus counts.

options.text: confuses the popularity of electric cars with their quality
options.why: Quality isn't discussed.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that Avalon sold far fewer cars in total this year
options.why: 40 percent of a small total can be fewer cars than 25 percent of a large one.

items.tldr: A bigger share of fewer total sales can mean fewer electric cars.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Electric cars' share rose from 25% to 40%.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: The conclusion is about a count, which depends on total sales too.

items.takeaway: Percentages alone can't establish amounts. Ask what happened to the total.

items.stimulus: To find out whether residents of Clearwater support building a new public pool, the city surveyed people leaving its existing community swim center. Ninety percent supported the new pool. Clearly, most Clearwater residents support it.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: assumes that residents who support the pool would use it
options.why: Use isn't part of the conclusion.

options.text: relies on a survey too small to be reliable
options.why: The survey's size isn't given; the problem is who was asked.

options.text: draws a conclusion about all residents from a group likely to be more favorable than residents in general
options.why: People at a swim center are likelier than average to want a pool.

options.text: treats a claim about the pool's popularity as a claim about its value
options.why: The conclusion is only about support.

options.text: fails to consider the cost of building the pool
options.why: The conclusion is about support, not cost.

items.tldr: Swimmers aren't a fair sample of residents on a pool question.

steps.label: Sample
steps.body: People leaving a swim center.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: They differ from residents in exactly the way that affects the answer.

items.takeaway: A biased sample can't support a conclusion about the whole population.

items.stimulus: Professor Okafor's study concludes that the city's new bus routes have shortened commute times. But Professor Okafor rides the bus to work every day, so her conclusion cannot be trusted.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses a correlation with a cause
options.why: No correlation is cited.

options.text: presumes that people who ride the bus prefer shorter commutes
options.why: Preferences aren't part of the argument.

options.text: assumes that commute time is the only measure of a bus system's success
options.why: The argument doesn't discuss measures of success.

options.text: dismisses a conclusion because of a fact about the person who reached it rather than the evidence for it
options.why: Riding the bus doesn't show her study's evidence is bad.

options.text: relies on a single study
options.why: The argument rejects the study rather than relying on it.

items.tldr: It attacks the researcher, not her research.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Conclusion: distrust the study. Reason: the author rides the bus.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: A personal connection can suggest checking the work, but it doesn't refute it.

items.takeaway: Rejecting a claim because of who made it is an ad hominem flaw.

items.stimulus: Children who eat breakfast every day earn higher grades than children who skip breakfast. So eating breakfast every day improves children's grades.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: presumes that what is true of children is true of adults
options.why: Adults aren't mentioned.

options.text: treats a claim about most children as a claim about every child
options.why: The comparison is between groups; no "every child" claim is made.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that some other factor, such as a structured home routine, leads both to daily breakfasts and to higher grades
options.why: A third factor could explain both, so the correlation doesn't show breakfast causes better grades.

options.text: assumes that all breakfasts are equally nutritious
options.why: The argument doesn't need that assumption.

options.text: relies on grades as the only measure of learning
options.why: The conclusion is about grades specifically.

items.tldr: A shared cause, like a stable home routine, could produce both breakfasts and grades.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Breakfast eaters get better grades.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: Correlation treated as cause. A common factor could produce both.

items.takeaway: Before accepting "X causes Y," look for a third factor that causes both.

items.stimulus: People who own dogs report being happier than people who do not. So owning a dog makes people happier.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses owning a dog with caring for a dog
options.why: That distinction plays no role.

options.text: ignores the possibility that happier people are more likely to choose to own dogs
options.why: The causation could run the other way.

options.text: assumes that dog owners own only one dog
options.why: The number of dogs doesn't matter here.

options.text: relies on self-reports that are known to be false
options.why: Nothing says the reports are false.

options.text: generalizes from dogs to all pets
options.why: The conclusion is only about dogs.

items.tldr: Maybe happiness leads to dog ownership, not the other way around.

steps.label: Claim
steps.body: Dogs → happiness.

steps.label: Alternative
steps.body: Happiness → choosing a dog explains the same correlation.

items.takeaway: For any "X causes Y" from a correlation, consider whether Y causes X.

items.stimulus: Critic: The science museum describes natural selection as a theory. But a theory is just a guess. So the museum admits that natural selection is only a guess.
items.prompt: The critic's reasoning is flawed because it

options.text: relies on a shift between a scientific and an everyday meaning of a key word
options.why: A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation; the everyday "theory" is a hunch.

options.text: treats the museum's description as the only evidence for natural selection
options.why: The argument says nothing about other evidence.

options.text: assumes that scientific claims can never be revised
options.why: Revision isn't discussed.

options.text: generalizes from one museum to all museums
options.why: The conclusion is about this museum's description.

options.text: rejects a claim because of who made it
options.why: The museum's credibility isn't attacked.

items.tldr: "Theory" means a tested explanation in science, not a guess.

steps.label: Key word
steps.body: "Theory."

steps.label: Two senses
steps.body: The museum uses the scientific sense; the critic substitutes the everyday sense.

items.takeaway: Equivocation hides in words with both technical and everyday meanings.

items.stimulus: The Riverside Review publishes only the finest poetry, because every poem it prints meets the highest standards. And we know the poems meet those standards because they appear in the Riverside Review.
items.prompt: The argument's reasoning is flawed because it

options.text: relies on the opinion of the journal's own editors
options.why: No editor is quoted.

options.text: confuses the quantity of poems with their quality
options.why: Quantity isn't discussed.

options.text: uses its conclusion as support for one of the claims offered in support of that conclusion
options.why: Appearing in the Review is used to prove quality, which is used to prove the Review's standards.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that other journals also publish fine poetry
options.why: The claim is about what the Review publishes, not about other journals.

options.text: assumes that popular poems are of high quality
options.why: Popularity isn't mentioned.

items.tldr: Good because it's in the Review; in the Review because it's good. That's a circle.

steps.label: Trace
steps.body: Finest poetry ← meets standards ← appears in the Review.

steps.label: Notice
steps.body: Appearing in the Review is exactly what's in question.

items.takeaway: Circular arguments return to their starting point without outside support.

items.stimulus: Ana: Either you support the new stadium or you don't care about our city's economy. You've said you oppose the stadium, so clearly you don't care about the economy.
items.prompt: The reasoning in Ana's argument is flawed because it

options.text: confuses the stadium's cost with its benefits
options.why: Costs and benefits aren't discussed.

options.text: generalizes from one city to all cities
options.why: Only one city is involved.

options.text: assumes that the stadium will be built
options.why: The argument doesn't predict whether it will be built.

options.text: relies on an authority on economics
options.why: No authority is cited.

options.text: presents two alternatives as the only possibilities when others exist
options.why: Someone can care about the economy and still oppose this stadium.

items.tldr: Opposing the stadium and caring about the economy are compatible.

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: Support it, or you don't care about the economy.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That ignores people who care about the economy but think the stadium is a bad deal.

items.takeaway: Test "either/or" claims by looking for someone who fits neither box.

items.stimulus: The famous actor Jonah Price uses Brightsmile toothpaste and says it is the best on the market. So Brightsmile must be the best toothpaste available.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: draws a conclusion about all toothpastes from one brand
options.why: The conclusion is about Brightsmile.

options.text: attacks the motives of a competing toothpaste maker
options.why: No competitor is mentioned.

options.text: confuses a product's price with its quality
options.why: Price isn't mentioned.

options.text: treats the endorsement of someone with no relevant expertise as proof of a claim
options.why: Being a famous actor doesn't make Price an expert on toothpaste.

options.text: assumes that the best toothpaste is also the most popular
options.why: Popularity isn't the argument's evidence.

items.tldr: A celebrity endorsement isn't expert evidence.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: An actor's personal preference.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: He has no expertise that would make his opinion strong evidence.

items.takeaway: Endorsements from non-experts are testimony, not proof.

items.stimulus: My grandfather smoked a pack of cigarettes a day and lived to be ninety-five. So smoking cannot be as harmful to health as doctors claim.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: appeals to the authority of doctors
options.why: The argument rejects the doctors' claim.

options.text: generalizes from all smokers to a single smoker
options.why: It runs the other way: one case is used against a general claim.

options.text: presumes that doctors have a financial motive to exaggerate
options.why: No motive is suggested.

options.text: treats a possible harm as if it were a certain harm
options.why: The argument does the reverse, discounting a likely harm.

options.text: relies on a single case to reject a claim about general tendencies
options.why: Doctors' claim is about risk across many people; one long-lived smoker doesn't refute it.

items.tldr: One exception doesn't disprove a general health risk.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: One smoker who lived long.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: General claims about risk survive individual exceptions.

items.takeaway: Anecdotes can't overturn claims about general tendencies.

items.stimulus: No one has ever shown that the old Harlow mansion is not haunted. So the mansion must be haunted.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: treats the failure to disprove a claim as proof that the claim is true
options.why: That nobody has disproved it isn't evidence that it's true.

options.text: attacks the credibility of skeptics
options.why: No skeptics are mentioned.

options.text: confuses a cause with its effect
options.why: No causal claim is made.

options.text: relies on the testimony of people who say they have seen ghosts
options.why: No testimony is cited.

options.text: assumes that what is true of one mansion is true of all old buildings
options.why: The conclusion concerns only this mansion.

items.tldr: "Not disproved" isn't "proved."

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: No evidence against the claim.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: The conclusion needs evidence for it.

items.takeaway: Lack of disproof, like lack of proof, settles nothing by itself.

items.stimulus: Most first-time novelists do not earn back their publisher's advance. Dana is a first-time novelist. So Dana will not earn back her advance.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: treats what is true of most members of a group as certain to be true of a particular member
options.why: "Most" leaves room for Dana to be one of the exceptions.

options.text: assumes that Dana's publisher is typical of all publishers
options.why: Even if her publisher is typical, "most" still doesn't guarantee Dana's result.

options.text: confuses earning back an advance with writing a good novel
options.why: Quality isn't discussed.

options.text: relies on statistics about advances that may be out of date
options.why: Nothing suggests the figures are outdated.

options.text: generalizes from a single novelist to all novelists
options.why: It runs the other way, applying a group statistic to one person.

items.tldr: "Most" makes Dana's outcome likely, not certain.

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: Most first-time novelists fall short.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: The conclusion says Dana definitely will, which needs "all."

items.takeaway: Statistical premises support probable conclusions, not certain ones.

items.stimulus: Residents of Marlow who drink at least two cups of green tea a day report fewer colds than residents who do not. Therefore, drinking green tea strengthens the immune system.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Green tea contains antioxidants that have shown health benefits in laboratory studies.
options.why: If anything this supports the argument. A weakener has to attack the link between the tea and the colds.

options.text: Coffee drinkers in Marlow report more colds than green tea drinkers do.
options.why: Coffee drinkers are a new group. Comparing them can't explain why tea drinkers get fewer colds.

options.text: Some residents who drink green tea daily still report catching colds.
options.why: The claim is that tea drinkers get fewer colds, not none. A few colds don't contradict it.

options.text: Marlow residents who drink green tea daily are also far more likely to exercise regularly and sleep at least seven hours a night.
options.why: It offers a rival cause for the fewer colds, so the tea may be a bystander.

options.text: The survey of Marlow residents was conducted during the winter.
options.why: Winter affects both groups alike, so it can't explain the gap between them.

items.tldr: A rival cause (exercise, sleep) explains the gap, not the tea.

steps.label: Task
steps.body: Weaken. Find the fact that most undermines the conclusion.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Evidence: tea drinkers report fewer colds. Conclusion: tea strengthens immunity.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: A correlation is treated as a cause. Prephrase: something else about tea drinkers keeps colds away.

items.takeaway: Arguments that jump from correlation to cause fall to a rival cause that differs between the groups.

items.stimulus: Over the past decade, the districts of Halverton with the most public libraries have had the lowest rates of juvenile crime. So building additional libraries in the districts with the highest rates of juvenile crime would reduce juvenile crime in those districts.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Juvenile crime in Halverton as a whole has declined over the past decade.
options.why: A citywide decline says nothing about why some districts have lower rates than others.

options.text: Most of Halverton's libraries were built more than thirty years ago.
options.why: The age of the buildings has no bearing on whether libraries reduce crime.

options.text: Some districts of Halverton with few public libraries also have low rates of juvenile crime.
options.why: A few exceptions don't undo a general pattern, and they don't show that libraries are irrelevant.

options.text: Libraries throughout Halverton have extended their evening hours in recent years.
options.why: The change applies to every district, so it can't account for differences between them.

options.text: The districts of Halverton with the most public libraries also have the highest household incomes and the most after-school programs.
options.why: Income and after-school programs are rival explanations for the low crime, so adding libraries alone might change nothing.

items.tldr: Wealth and after-school programs could explain the low crime, so more libraries may not help.

steps.label: Task
steps.body: Weaken a prediction that rests on a correlation.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Evidence: more libraries go with less juvenile crime. Conclusion: adding libraries will cut crime.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: It assumes the libraries cause the low crime. Prephrase: something else about those districts keeps crime low.

items.takeaway: When a plan copies one feature of a successful group, look for the other features that group has.

items.stimulus: Patients at Elmridge Clinic who used a new mobile reminder app took their medication on schedule far more consistently than patients who did not use the app. The clinic's director concludes that the app causes patients to take their medication more consistently.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's argument?

options.text: Before the app was introduced, the patients who later chose to use it had been no more consistent in taking their medication than other patients.
options.why: It rules out the main alternative: that the app users were already the more consistent patients.

options.text: Many clinics other than Elmridge have also begun recommending mobile reminder apps.
options.why: Other clinics' recommendations aren't evidence about this app's effect.

options.text: Patients who did not use the app were more likely to report unpleasant side effects from their medication.
options.why: That's a rival reason the non-users skipped doses, so it weakens the argument.

options.text: The app was developed by a company that also manufactures medication.
options.why: Who made the app says nothing about whether it changes patients' behavior.

options.text: Some patients who used the app nonetheless missed several doses of their medication.
options.why: The claim is about consistency compared with other patients. Some missed doses are expected either way.

items.tldr: Showing both groups started out equally consistent rules out self-selection.

steps.label: Task
steps.body: Strengthen a causal conclusion drawn from a comparison.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: App users were more consistent than non-users, so the app caused the consistency.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: The users chose the app. Maybe the more conscientious patients are the ones who chose it.

steps.label: Fix
steps.body: Show the two groups were alike before the app arrived.

items.takeaway: To strengthen "X caused the difference," show the groups were alike before X.

items.stimulus: Critic: The novel Tidewater should not be assigned in introductory literature courses. Its plot turns on several historical events that most first-year students have never heard of, so those students would miss the point of the novel's central conflict.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the critic's argument depends?

options.text: Tidewater is the only novel whose plot turns on unfamiliar historical events.
options.why: Other novels could share the problem. The argument doesn't depend on Tidewater being unique.

options.text: Advanced literature courses are a better place for novels with complex plots.
options.why: The critic never says where the novel should be assigned, so this isn't required.

options.text: Novels assigned in introductory literature courses should contain no historical references at all.
options.why: The argument doesn't need to ban every reference, only the kind that blocks understanding.

options.text: Most first-year students would enjoy Tidewater if they understood its historical references.
options.why: The argument is about understanding the conflict, not enjoyment.

options.text: Tidewater does not itself provide enough information about those historical events for an unfamiliar reader to grasp its central conflict.
options.why: Negate it: if the novel explains the events itself, students wouldn't miss the point and the argument collapses.

items.tldr: If the novel explained the history itself, students wouldn't miss the point, so the argument needs it not to.

steps.label: Task
steps.body: Necessary assumption. Find what the argument can't survive without.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Evidence: students don't know the history. Conclusion: they'd miss the novel's point, so don't assign it.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: Not knowing history beforehand only matters if the book doesn't fill it in.

steps.label: Check
steps.body: Negate the answer. If Tidewater explains the events, the argument fails.

items.takeaway: Use the negation test. A necessary assumption, once negated, breaks the argument.

items.stimulus: Anyone who qualifies for the Morrow Fellowship has published original research. Dana has not published any original research. Therefore, Dana is not eligible for the faculty travel grant.
items.prompt: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

options.text: Only people who qualify for the Morrow Fellowship are eligible for the faculty travel grant.
options.why: Grant → Fellowship → published. Dana hasn't published, so Dana can't qualify, so Dana isn't eligible.

options.text: Anyone who has published original research is eligible for the faculty travel grant.
options.why: This tells us who is eligible, not who isn't. It can't rule Dana out.

options.text: Anyone who qualifies for the Morrow Fellowship is eligible for the faculty travel grant.
options.why: That's Fellowship → grant, the wrong direction. We need grant → Fellowship.

options.text: Dana has applied for the Morrow Fellowship in the past.
options.why: Applying says nothing about qualifying or about the grant.

options.text: Most people who are eligible for the faculty travel grant have published original research.
options.why: "Most" leaves room for Dana to be eligible anyway, so the conclusion isn't guaranteed.

items.tldr: If only Fellowship-qualified people can get the grant, Dana (unpublished, so not qualified) can't get it.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Premise: Fellowship → published. Contrapositive: not published → not Fellowship.

steps.label: Apply
steps.body: Dana hasn't published, so Dana doesn't qualify for the Fellowship.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: The conclusion is about the travel grant, a new term. We need: not Fellowship → not grant, which is the same as grant → Fellowship.

items.takeaway: "Only X are Y" means Y → X. In sufficient assumption questions, the right answer chains the new term to the premises in the needed direction.

items.stimulus: Every successful restaurant in Lindale advertises on local radio. Café Orla advertises on local radio, so it will surely be successful.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: assumes that what is true of restaurants in Lindale is true of restaurants everywhere
options.why: The conclusion stays in Lindale; it never generalizes beyond it.

options.text: confuses a cause of a restaurant's success with an effect of it
options.why: The argument makes no causal claim, only a conditional one, so this isn't the mistake.

options.text: relies on too small a sample of restaurants to support a general conclusion
options.why: The premise covers every successful restaurant. Sample size isn't the issue.

options.text: takes for granted that a condition required for success is enough to guarantee it
options.why: Radio ads are necessary for success in Lindale, not sufficient. Plenty of failing restaurants might advertise too.

options.text: attacks the reputation of Café Orla instead of evaluating its advertising
options.why: The argument says nothing about Café Orla's reputation.

items.tldr: Advertising is required for success, but the argument treats it as a guarantee.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Premise: successful → advertises. The argument concludes: advertises → successful.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That reverses the conditional, treating a necessary condition as a sufficient one.

items.takeaway: "All successful X do Y" never means "doing Y makes X successful."

items.stimulus: Each of the five programs in the Kestrel software suite runs quickly on older computers. So the Kestrel suite, with all five programs running at once, will run quickly on older computers.
items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument?

options.text: It relies on testimony from the software's developers.
options.why: No testimony appears in the argument.

options.text: It treats one possible cause of slow performance as the only cause.
options.why: The argument never identifies a cause of slowness.

options.text: It draws a conclusion about all computers from evidence about older computers.
options.why: The conclusion is about older computers only.

options.text: It presumes that what is true of a whole is true of each of its parts.
options.why: That's the division flaw, the mirror image. Here the reasoning runs part → whole.

options.text: It presumes that what is true of each part of a whole is true of the whole.
options.why: Programs that are fast alone can be slow together, since they compete for the same memory and processor.

items.tldr: Five fast programs can still be slow when they run together.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Each part (program) is fast, so the whole (the suite running together) must be fast.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That's composition: properties of parts don't automatically transfer to the whole.

items.takeaway: Composition assumes parts → whole. Division assumes whole → parts. Both are flaws.

items.stimulus: Every Brennan College student who studies abroad must first complete two years of a foreign language. Of the Brennan students who were eligible to study abroad this year, fewer than half chose to do so. Even so, the number of Brennan students studying abroad this year is the highest in the college's history.
items.prompt: If the statements above are true, which one of the following is most strongly supported by them?

options.text: Fewer Brennan students are studying abroad this year than in some previous year.
options.why: This year's number is the highest ever, so this contradicts the stimulus.

options.text: This year, more than twice as many Brennan students were eligible to study abroad as actually did so.
options.why: Everyone who went was eligible, and fewer than half of the eligible went, so eligible students outnumber those who went by more than two to one.

options.text: Most Brennan students who complete two years of a foreign language do not want to study abroad.
options.why: Choosing not to go isn't the same as not wanting to. Cost or scheduling could explain it.

options.text: Brennan College recently increased its foreign language requirement.
options.why: Nothing in the stimulus mentions a change in the requirement.

options.text: More Brennan students were eligible to study abroad this year than in any previous year.
options.why: Tempting, but a past year could have had more eligible students and a lower participation rate.

items.tldr: All who went were eligible, and under half of the eligible went, so eligible students outnumber them more than two to one.

steps.label: Task
steps.body: Most strongly supported. Find what the facts prove, not what's merely likely.

steps.label: Combine
steps.body: Students abroad ⊆ eligible students, and abroad < ½ × eligible. So eligible > 2 × abroad.

steps.label: Trap
steps.body: A record number abroad doesn't mean a record number eligible. Counts and rates can move independently.

items.takeaway: Proportions constrain counts. "Fewer than half went" means non-goers outnumber goers, but a record count of goers doesn't imply a record pool.

items.stimulus: Some economists argue that raising the minimum wage always reduces employment. But this view cannot be right. Several regions that raised their minimum wage last year saw employment grow, and economists who study those regions found no evidence that employment would have grown faster without the increase.
items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the argument?

options.text: Economists who study regional employment are more reliable than other economists.
options.why: The argument never compares the reliability of economists.

options.text: Raising the minimum wage never reduces employment.
options.why: The author denies "always reduces," which is not the same as claiming "never reduces."

options.text: It is not the case that raising the minimum wage always reduces employment.
options.why: That's the claim "this view cannot be right," spelled out. Everything after it is evidence for it.

options.text: Employment grew last year in several regions that raised their minimum wage.
options.why: This is evidence the author offers, not what the evidence is meant to show.

options.text: Raising the minimum wage tends to increase employment.
options.why: The author only shows that raises don't always cut jobs, not that they usually add them.

items.tldr: The conclusion is the rejection itself: raising the minimum wage doesn't always reduce employment.

steps.label: Find
steps.body: "But this view cannot be right" is the author's position. Translate "this view" back into words.

steps.label: Check
steps.body: The regional data support it, so they're premises, not the conclusion.

steps.label: Calibrate
steps.body: Denying "always" isn't asserting "never." Keep the answer exactly that strong.

items.takeaway: When an author rejects someone else's view, the rejection is usually the main conclusion. Match its strength exactly.

items.stimulus: Museum director: Some board members want to charge admission to pay for new exhibits. But an admission fee would discourage the students and low-income families our charter obliges us to serve. Admittedly, a fee would raise substantial revenue. Still, we should fund the exhibits through private donations instead.
items.prompt: The claim that a fee would raise substantial revenue plays which one of the following roles in the director's argument?

options.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
options.why: The conclusion is that the museum should seek private donations instead.

options.text: It is an intermediate conclusion supported by the claim about the museum's charter.
options.why: The charter point supports the main conclusion, not the revenue claim.

options.text: It is a claim that the director tries to show is false.
options.why: The director accepts the claim. She just thinks other factors outweigh it.

options.text: It is offered as direct support for the argument's conclusion.
options.why: Revenue from a fee argues for the fee, not for seeking donations instead.

options.text: It is a consideration the director concedes that might seem to count against the conclusion.
options.why: "Admittedly" signals a concession: revenue is a point in the fee's favor that the director acknowledges.

items.tldr: "Admittedly" marks a concession: revenue counts against the conclusion, and the director grants it.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Conclusion: fund exhibits through donations. Support: a fee would deter those the charter requires serving.

steps.label: Role
steps.body: The revenue claim points the other way, and the director grants it before rejecting the fee anyway.

items.takeaway: Concession signals ("admittedly," "granted," "although") mark points the author accepts but argues past.

items.stimulus: After the town of Pell installed brighter streetlights on its main roads, the number of nighttime traffic accidents on those roads increased, even though the brighter lights make it easier for drivers to see.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?

options.text: Most residents of Pell approved of the decision to install the new lights.
options.why: Residents' approval doesn't explain the accident numbers.

options.text: The brighter streetlights cost more to operate than the old ones did.
options.why: Operating cost has nothing to do with the number of accidents.

options.text: Several other towns that installed brighter streetlights saw nighttime accidents decrease.
options.why: That makes Pell's increase more surprising, not less.

options.text: Brighter streetlights also make it easier for pedestrians to see oncoming cars.
options.why: Another safety benefit makes the rise in accidents even more puzzling.

options.text: After the new lights were installed, many drivers who had avoided Pell's main roads at night began using them, greatly increasing nighttime traffic.
options.why: More cars on the road can mean more accidents in total, even if each driver sees better.

items.tldr: Better visibility can coexist with more accidents if many more people drive at night.

steps.label: Facts
steps.body: Brighter lights improve visibility, yet nighttime accidents rose.

steps.label: Prephrase
steps.body: Something else changed: more drivers, faster driving, or more risk-taking.

steps.label: Check
steps.body: The right answer keeps both facts true. More traffic does that: the rate per driver can fall while the total rises.

items.takeaway: Resolve a paradox by explaining how both facts hold. Totals can rise while per-person rates fall.

items.stimulus: Columnist: The city should not adopt the proposed downtown parking rules. Although the rules would ease traffic congestion, they would make it much harder for disabled residents to reach the medical offices located downtown.
items.prompt: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the columnist's reasoning?

options.text: A city should adopt any policy that would ease congestion downtown.
options.why: This supports adopting the rules, the opposite of the columnist's conclusion.

options.text: No policy should be adopted unless every resident supports it.
options.why: The columnist's argument is about access to medical care, not unanimous support.

options.text: A policy that would significantly impede disabled residents' access to medical care should not be adopted, even if it has other benefits.
options.why: It matches the evidence (harder access to medical offices) to the conclusion (don't adopt), even granting the congestion benefit.

options.text: Congestion downtown is a more serious problem than limited access to medical offices.
options.why: This would favor adopting the rules.

options.text: Cities should provide more parking near medical offices than near other businesses.
options.why: This doesn't address whether these particular rules should be rejected.

items.tldr: The principle has to say that harming disabled residents' access to care outweighs the congestion benefit.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Benefit: less congestion. Cost: disabled residents lose access to care. Conclusion: don't adopt.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: The principle should rank that cost above that benefit, specifically and without overreaching.

items.takeaway: A justifying principle connects this argument's evidence to its conclusion, and doesn't go further.

items.stimulus: If Lena takes the overnight train, she will arrive before the conference begins. If she arrives before the conference begins, she will give the opening talk. But Lena will not give the opening talk. So Lena will not take the overnight train.
items.prompt: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

options.text: If the bakery does not open early, it will not sell out by noon. The bakery will not open early. So the owner will not bake a second batch.
options.why: Its premises and conclusion don't line up with the original's chain-and-denial pattern.

options.text: If the bakery opens early, it will sell out by noon, and if it sells out by noon, the owner will bake a second batch. So if the owner bakes a second batch, the bakery opened early.
options.why: It reverses the chain's direction instead of denying its end.

options.text: If the bakery opens early, it will sell out of bread by noon. If it sells out by noon, the owner will bake a second batch. The owner will not bake a second batch. So the bakery will not open early.
options.why: Same chain (P → Q, Q → R), same denial of the last link (not R), same valid conclusion (not P).

options.text: The bakery will open early only if it sells out by noon. The bakery will sell out by noon. So the bakery will open early.
options.why: "Only if" introduces a necessary condition. Meeting it doesn't guarantee the bakery opens early.

options.text: If the bakery opens early, it will sell out of bread by noon. The bakery will sell out of bread by noon. So the bakery will open early.
options.why: This affirms the result to conclude the condition, which is invalid. The original is valid.

items.tldr: Deny the chain's end to deny its start: P→Q→R, not R, so not P. Only one bakery argument copies that exactly.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Overnight train → arrive early → opening talk. Not opening talk. So not overnight train.

steps.label: Abstract
steps.body: P → Q, Q → R, not R, therefore not P. That's a valid chained contrapositive.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Find the same links and the same move. Ignore the topic entirely.

items.takeaway: Parallel questions test structure. Translate the stimulus into letters, then find the answer with the same letters.

items.stimulus: Every licensed pilot has passed a vision test. Marco has passed a vision test. So Marco must be a licensed pilot.
items.prompt: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

options.text: Some first-aid instructors are certified lifeguards. Priya is a first-aid instructor. So Priya is a certified lifeguard.
options.why: Flawed, but it misuses "some," a different error from the original's reversal.

options.text: Every certified lifeguard has completed a first-aid course. Priya is a certified lifeguard. So Priya has completed a first-aid course.
options.why: This applies the rule correctly. It's valid.

options.text: Most certified lifeguards are strong swimmers. Priya is a certified lifeguard. So Priya is probably a strong swimmer.
options.why: A cautious probabilistic inference, not the reversal in the original.

options.text: Every certified lifeguard has completed a first-aid course. Priya has not completed a first-aid course. So Priya is not a certified lifeguard.
options.why: This is the valid contrapositive, so there's no flaw to match.

options.text: Every certified lifeguard has completed a first-aid course. Priya has completed a first-aid course. So Priya must be a certified lifeguard.
options.why: Same flaw: meeting a requirement is treated as proof of belonging to the group.

items.tldr: The original treats a requirement (passing a vision test) as a guarantee. Only the argument that treats a first-aid course as proof of being a lifeguard makes the same mistake.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Pilot → passed test. Marco passed the test. So Marco is a pilot.

steps.label: Name the flaw
steps.body: It reverses the conditional, treating a necessary condition as sufficient.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Find the answer with the same reversal. Valid arguments can't match a flawed one.

items.takeaway: In parallel flaw questions, name the flaw first, then eliminate every answer that's valid or flawed in a different way.

items.stimulus:
Amara: The city's new bike lanes have made downtown streets safer. Serious collisions there have dropped by a third since the lanes opened.
Desmond: The drop in collisions isn't due to the bike lanes. The city lowered the downtown speed limit at the same time, and slower traffic alone would explain the decline.
items.prompt: Amara and Desmond disagree over whether

options.text: the bike lanes are responsible for the decline in serious collisions downtown
options.why: Amara credits the bike lanes; Desmond credits the lower speed limit instead.

options.text: the downtown speed limit should be lowered further
options.why: Neither speaker says anything about lowering it further.

options.text: serious collisions downtown have declined since the bike lanes opened
options.why: Desmond accepts the decline. He disputes its cause.

options.text: the city should build more bike lanes
options.why: Neither speaker makes a recommendation.

options.text: bike lanes make streets safer in every city
options.why: Both speakers talk only about this city's downtown.

items.tldr: They agree collisions fell; they disagree about whether the bike lanes caused it.

steps.label: Amara
steps.body: Collisions fell, and the bike lanes made the streets safer.

steps.label: Desmond
steps.body: Collisions fell, but the lower speed limit, not the lanes, explains it.

steps.label: Test
steps.body: The answer must be something both address and disagree on. Only the cause qualifies.

items.takeaway: For disagreement questions, check each answer against both speakers. Each must have a view, and the views must conflict.

items.stimulus: Critic: The mayor claims that no public project in this city has ever been finished on time. But the Harbor Bridge, a public project, opened two months ahead of schedule.
items.prompt: The critic responds to the mayor's claim by

options.text: showing that the mayor's claim contradicts itself
options.why: The claim is contradicted by a fact, not by itself.

options.text: offering a counterexample to a general claim
options.why: One project finished early is enough to refute "no public project has ever been on time."

options.text: arguing that most public projects in the city are finished on time
options.why: The critic cites one project. That says nothing about most projects.

options.text: questioning the mayor's motives for making the claim
options.why: The critic never mentions the mayor's motives.

options.text: providing evidence that the Harbor Bridge cost less than projected
options.why: Cost is never mentioned. The point is the schedule.

items.tldr: A single on-time project refutes "no project has ever been on time." That's a counterexample.

steps.label: Claim
steps.body: Mayor: no public project here has ever been finished on time.

steps.label: Reply
steps.body: The critic names one public project that was early.

steps.label: Method
steps.body: One counterexample defeats a universal claim.

items.takeaway: "Never" and "always" claims fall to a single counterexample, but one example doesn't prove the opposite generalization.

items.stimulus: Since the town of Brook Falls began offering free swimming lessons for children, drowning incidents involving children there have fallen sharply. So the free lessons have made children in Brook Falls safer around water.
items.prompt: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

options.text: How many adults in Brook Falls know how to swim
options.why: The argument is about children; adult swimming ability doesn't test the causal claim.

options.text: Whether Brook Falls began posting lifeguards at its public beaches when the lessons began
options.why: If yes, lifeguards are a rival cause and the argument weakens. If no, a major alternative is ruled out and it strengthens.

options.text: Whether other towns near Brook Falls offer swimming lessons for adults
options.why: Adult lessons in other towns don't bear on what caused Brook Falls' decline.

options.text: Whether most children in Brook Falls enjoy swimming
options.why: Enjoyment doesn't affect whether the lessons caused the drop in drownings.

options.text: Whether drowning incidents are more common in summer than in winter
options.why: Seasonal patterns apply before and after the lessons alike.

items.tldr: Knowing whether lifeguards arrived at the same time would either rule out or reveal a rival cause.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Drownings fell after free lessons began, so the lessons made children safer.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: Something else that changed at the same time could explain the drop.

steps.label: Test
steps.body: The right question has an answer that matters either way. Lifeguards does.

items.takeaway: An evaluate answer is a question whose answer would strengthen the argument one way and weaken it the other.

items.stimulus: Every member of the debate team takes a logic course. No one who takes a logic course is exempt from the writing requirement. Carla is exempt from the writing requirement.
items.prompt: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

options.text: Carla does not take any courses.
options.why: We only know she doesn't take a logic course.

options.text: Some members of the debate team are exempt from the writing requirement.
options.why: Every debate member takes logic, and no logic student is exempt.

options.text: Carla is not a member of the debate team.
options.why: Exempt → no logic course → not on the debate team (two contrapositives chained).

options.text: Carla takes a logic course but is not on the debate team.
options.why: Logic students aren't exempt, and Carla is, so she can't take logic.

options.text: Everyone who takes a logic course is a member of the debate team.
options.why: That reverses "debate team → logic course."

items.tldr: Exempt → no logic course → not on the debate team.

steps.label: Chain
steps.body: Debate → logic → not exempt.

steps.label: Contrapositive
steps.body: Exempt → not logic → not debate.

steps.label: Apply
steps.body: Carla is exempt, so she isn't on the debate team.

items.takeaway: Chain the conditionals, then run the contrapositive backward from the fact you're given.

items.stimulus: Dr. Reyes argues that the new zoning plan will raise housing costs. But Dr. Reyes owns several rental properties in the city, so her argument should be dismissed.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: fails to explain why the zoning plan was proposed
options.why: The plan's origins aren't relevant to the flaw.

options.text: relies on the opinion of a single expert
options.why: It doesn't rely on her opinion; it dismisses it.

options.text: assumes that housing costs will rise regardless of the zoning plan
options.why: The argument makes no prediction about housing costs.

options.text: confuses a cause of rising housing costs with an effect of them
options.why: No causal claim is made.

options.text: rejects an argument because of a fact about the person making it rather than the argument's merits
options.why: Owning rentals might give her a motive, but it says nothing about whether she's right.

items.tldr: It dismisses her argument because of who she is, not what she argues.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Conclusion: dismiss Dr. Reyes's argument. Reason: she owns rental properties.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: A possible bias doesn't make an argument wrong. The argument never addresses her evidence.

items.takeaway: Attacking the arguer (ad hominem) is a flaw. Motives can raise suspicion but can't refute reasoning.

items.stimulus: A survey of members of the Riverside Cycling Club found that 85 percent support adding bike lanes to Main Street. So most residents of Riverside support adding bike lanes to Main Street.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Members of the Riverside Cycling Club ride bicycles far more often than most Riverside residents do.
options.why: The sample differs from residents in exactly the way that shapes views on bike lanes, so it isn't representative.

options.text: The survey was conducted by the club's own volunteers.
options.why: It hints at bias but doesn't show the results misrepresent residents.

options.text: Bike lanes have been added to streets in several nearby towns.
options.why: Other towns don't tell us what Riverside residents think.

options.text: Some club members do not live on Main Street.
options.why: The conclusion is about Riverside residents, not Main Street residents.

options.text: Most club members who support the bike lanes also support wider sidewalks.
options.why: Views on sidewalks don't affect whether the sample represents residents.

items.tldr: Cyclists aren't typical residents, so a cycling club can't speak for the town on bike lanes.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Club members support bike lanes, so most residents do.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: It assumes club members represent all residents.

steps.label: Attack
steps.body: Show the sample differs in a way that matters. Frequent cyclists do.

items.takeaway: Survey arguments fall when the sample differs from the population in a way that bears on the question asked.

items.stimulus: Library director: Our new self-checkout kiosks will reduce the time patrons wait in line. After all, patrons who use the kiosks won't need to wait for a staff member to check out their books.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the director's argument?

options.text: At least some patrons will use the self-checkout kiosks rather than wait for a staff member.
options.why: Negate it and no one uses the kiosks, so lines can't get shorter.

options.text: Staff members will be reassigned to other tasks once the kiosks are installed.
options.why: The argument doesn't need this, and if true it might lengthen lines.

options.text: The kiosks cost less to operate than hiring more staff would.
options.why: Cost has nothing to do with waiting time.

options.text: Every patron who uses the kiosks will finish checking out in under a minute.
options.why: Kiosks can help without every checkout being that fast.

options.text: Most patrons prefer self-checkout to checking out with a staff member.
options.why: Even a minority using the kiosks could shorten lines. "Most" isn't required.

items.tldr: If nobody uses the kiosks, waiting time can't fall, so the argument needs some to use them.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Kiosk users skip the staff line, so waiting time will fall.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: That only works if someone actually uses the kiosks.

steps.label: Check
steps.body: Negate the right answer ("no patrons use them") and the argument collapses.

items.takeaway: Necessary assumptions are often modest ("at least some"). Answers with "most" or "every" usually ask for more than the argument needs.

items.stimulus: After the Greenvale school district began serving breakfast to all students at no cost, the district's average attendance rose by four percentage points. The superintendent concludes that the free breakfast program improved attendance.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the superintendent's argument?

options.text: Attendance in neighboring districts that did not offer free breakfast stayed the same over the same period.
options.why: It rules out a regional trend that would have raised attendance anyway.

options.text: Some students who eat the free breakfast still miss school occasionally.
options.why: The claim is about average attendance; some absences are expected either way.

options.text: The free breakfast program has cost the district more than expected.
options.why: Cost doesn't bear on whether breakfast improved attendance.

options.text: Greenvale also began a new attendance-reward program that year.
options.why: That's a rival cause, so it weakens the argument.

options.text: Many Greenvale students had already been eating breakfast at home before the program began.
options.why: If many already ate breakfast, the program changed less, which undercuts it.

items.tldr: If similar districts without free breakfast saw no change, the breakfast is the likelier cause.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Free breakfast began, then attendance rose, so breakfast raised attendance.

steps.label: Alternatives
steps.body: A regional trend or another new program could explain the rise.

steps.label: Fix
steps.body: A comparison group without the program, and without the rise, rules out a trend.

items.takeaway: A comparison group that didn't get the change, and didn't improve, is one of the strongest strengtheners for a causal claim.

items.stimulus: The share of Fairport's budget spent on parks fell from 6 percent last year to 5 percent this year. Clearly, Fairport is spending less money on its parks than it did last year.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because it

options.text: assumes that parks are the most important part of the budget
options.why: The argument says nothing about importance.

options.text: confuses the number of parks with the amount spent on them
options.why: The number of parks is never mentioned.

options.text: takes for granted that spending on parks should never decrease
options.why: No such value judgment appears.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that Fairport's total budget grew enough that 5 percent of it is more money than 6 percent of last year's budget
options.why: A smaller share of a bigger budget can still be more money.

options.text: compares figures from only two years
options.why: Comparing two years is fine. The problem is mixing shares with amounts.

items.tldr: A smaller percentage of a larger budget can be more dollars.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The parks' share of the budget fell from 6% to 5%.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Parks are getting less money.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: It ignores the size of the total. Percentages alone can't show amounts.

items.takeaway: When evidence is a percentage and the conclusion is an amount (or the reverse), check whether the total changed.

items.stimulus: A hospital installed hand-sanitizer stations outside every patient room, and staff used them far more often than they had used the old sinks. Yet the number of reported hospital-acquired infections rose over the following year.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy?

options.text: Sanitizer kills many of the germs that cause hospital-acquired infections.
options.why: That makes a rise in infections more surprising, not less.

options.text: The number of patients the hospital treated stayed the same.
options.why: It rules out patient volume as an explanation, so the puzzle remains.

options.text: Staff at many other hospitals also use sanitizer stations.
options.why: Other hospitals don't explain this hospital's numbers.

options.text: Hand sanitizer is less expensive than soap and water.
options.why: Cost doesn't explain the rise in reported infections.

options.text: When the stations were installed, the hospital began testing every patient for infections, so many infections that once went undetected were now reported.
options.why: Reported infections can rise even if actual infections fell, because more are being found.

items.tldr: Wider testing made more infections visible, so reported numbers rose despite better hygiene.

steps.label: Facts
steps.body: Hand hygiene improved, yet reported infections rose.

steps.label: Notice
steps.body: The stimulus says "reported." Reporting can change even if reality doesn't.

steps.label: Resolve
steps.body: More testing finds more cases, which reconciles both facts.

items.takeaway: Watch for "reported" or "recorded" in paradoxes. A change in measurement can explain a surprising rise.

items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

options.text: Legal documents should avoid all technical terms so that consumers can understand them.
options.why: The author never calls for banning all technical terms.

options.text: Archaic legal phrases were litigated repeatedly during the twentieth century.
options.why: That's one detail from the second paragraph, not the main point.

options.text: Although traditional legal drafting was defended as precise, plain language need not sacrifice precision, which depends more on careful drafting than on vocabulary.
options.why: It covers the traditional view, the movement's challenge and the author's own conclusion in the final paragraph.

options.text: Jurisdictions that require plain-language contracts have fewer legal disputes than those that do not.
options.why: The passage never compares dispute rates across jurisdictions.

options.text: The plain-language movement has failed because critics still claim that plain language sacrifices precision.
options.why: The critics' persistence isn't presented as the movement's failure.

items.tldr: The passage moves from the traditional defense to the author's claim that precision comes from careful drafting, not archaic words.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1: the traditional style and its defense. P2: the movement's challenge. P3: critics answered, then the author's lesson.

steps.label: Author
steps.body: The author's own view is in P3: clarity and precision aren't really at odds.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: The right answer has to reach that conclusion, not stop at a detail.

items.takeaway: A main-point answer covers the whole passage and lands on the author's own position.

items.prompt: The author mentions that many supposedly settled phrases "had in fact been litigated repeatedly" (second paragraph) primarily in order to

options.text: illustrate the archaic vocabulary of traditional legal documents
options.why: The vocabulary examples come in the first paragraph. This detail does a different job.

options.text: concede a point to critics of the plain-language movement
options.why: It's a point against the traditional style, made by the movement's advocates.

options.text: undermine the defenders' claim that traditional phrases had settled meanings
options.why: If the phrases kept ending up in court, their meanings weren't settled, which is exactly what the defenders claimed.

options.text: show that plain-language documents produce less litigation
options.why: The detail is about traditional phrases, not plain-language documents.

options.text: suggest that courts have been hostile to the plain-language movement
options.why: Nothing in the passage describes courts' attitude toward the movement.

items.tldr: Repeated litigation shows the "settled" meanings weren't settled, rebutting the defenders.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The detail opens P2, where advocates "challenged this view," meaning the defenders' view from P1.

steps.label: Purpose
steps.body: The defenders said meanings were settled. Repeated lawsuits suggest otherwise.

items.takeaway: For function questions, ask what claim the detail supports or undercuts in its paragraph.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward the critics described in the third paragraph can most accurately be described as

options.text: complete indifference
options.why: The author takes the time to rebut them.

options.text: open contempt
options.why: Nothing in the tone is scornful.

options.text: reluctant acceptance
options.why: The author doesn't accept the critics' claim.

options.text: measured disagreement
options.why: The author rejects their claim ("less at odds than the critics suppose") without hostility.

options.text: respectful agreement
options.why: The author argues against the critics with "Yet…"

items.tldr: "Yet clarity and precision are less at odds than the critics suppose" is polite disagreement.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: P3 presents the critics, then pivots with "Yet."

steps.label: Calibrate
steps.body: The author disagrees, but calmly. Extreme tones like contempt overshoot.

items.takeaway: RC authors rarely sneer. When an author disagrees, pick the measured answer over the extreme one.

items.prompt: According to the passage, defenders of the traditional style argued that

options.text: changing tested wording could invite litigation over the meaning of new words
options.why: The first paragraph says exactly this.

options.text: legal documents should be read only by lawyers
options.why: The passage never attributes this to anyone.

options.text: plain language is too informal for use in court
options.why: The critics in P3 worry about precision, not formality, and they aren't the defenders.

options.text: archaic terms are more elegant than everyday language
